suppliers.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, an integer $r\ge1$, and an action scale
$\hbar>0$. Inner products are linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Use the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ of
[[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]]. In Schrödinger coordinates
define the self-adjoint quadratures
$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$
where $x_j$ is the real multiplication operator on its maximal domain and
$-i\partial_{x_j}$ is defined by conjugating that multiplication operator by
the unitary Fourier transform. Their common Schwartz core satisfies
$$[Q_j,Q_k]=[P_j,P_k]=0,\qquad [Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I.$$
Write $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$ and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Weyl unitary labelled by $z=(q_1,p_1,\ldots,q_r,p_r)$ is the unitary
whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$, is
$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
It obeys $W(z)W(z')=e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}W(z+z')$ and is regular and
irreducible. By the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem, every
nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this
same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n \langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$, for $r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$,
define the Weyl unitaries in grouped label order $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^r\oplus
\mathbb R^r$ by
$$[W(q,p)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
For $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$, every
$T\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ has a unitary $M_T$ such that
$$M_T^*W(z)M_T=W(Tz)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}).$$
Any two such unitaries differ by a scalar of modulus one. The covariance
identity holds on all of $L^2$; the corresponding unbounded quadrature
identities hold on the common transported Schwartz domain. This is an
individual existence and phase-uniqueness result; it does not identify the
global topology or kernel of a continuously chosen implementer family.

Let $r\ge1$, $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$, and
$$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)=\{S\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R):S^TJ_0S=J_0\}.$$
Every $S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is a finite product of matrices
of the following three types and their inverses:
$$U_X=\begin{pmatrix}I&X\\0&I\end{pmatrix},\quad L_Y=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\Y&I\end{pmatrix},\quad D_A=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&A^{-T}\end{pmatrix},$$
where $X,Y$ are real symmetric and $A$ is real invertible. Partial Fourier
rotations, which act by $(q_j,p_j)\mapsto(-p_j,q_j)$ on any selected set of
coordinates and fix the others, are also products of these matrices.
In addition, for every $S$ there is a product $G$ of these generators such
that the upper-left block of $SG$ is invertible.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Fix a measurable integrable representative, also denoted by $f$, if $L^1([a,b])$ is interpreted as a space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then there is a measurable set $E\subseteq(a,b)$ whose complement in $(a,b)$ has Lebesgue measure zero such that $F$ is differentiable at every $x\in E$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in E).$$
The primitive $F$ is independent of the chosen representative; the almost-everywhere derivative identity holds for every fixed measurable integrable representative.
